records.answer_text: In the context of LLMs, RAG stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation. It is a technique in which a large language model first retrieves relevant documents or data from an external knowledge source (e.g., a vector database, document store, or search engine) and then incorporates that retrieved content into its prompt to generate a grounded response. This lets the model use domain-specific or up-to-date information not present in its training data, reduces hallucinations, allows source citation, and avoids costly retraining. The term was introduced in the 2020 paper by Lewis et al. (Facebook AI Research), which combined a parametric language model with a non-parametric external memory accessed via retrieval at inference time. A standard RAG pipeline has three stages: retrieval, augmentation (adding retrieved context to the prompt), and generation.
records.counterfactual: Inverted hypothesis: 'RAG' in the LLM context stands for something other than Retrieval-Augmented Generation (e.g., a different expansion of the acronym), or the term did not originate with the 2020 Lewis et al. paper. Verdict: COLLAPSES — Wikipedia, multiple peer-reviewed arXiv papers, industry documentation (Weaviate), and a PMC medical study all independently and consistently expand RAG as Retrieval-Augmented Generation and attribute its introduction to Lewis et al. 2020; no credible source offers an alternative expansion within the LLM domain.

records.answer_text: MAST (Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy), introduced by Cemri et al. (UC Berkeley, 2025) in the paper 'Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?' (arXiv 2503.13657), defines 14 distinct failure modes. These are clustered into 3 top-level categories: (1) system design / specification issues (FM-1.x, e.g., disobey task specification, disobey role specification, step repetition, loss of conversation history, unaware of termination conditions), (2) inter-agent misalignment (FM-2.x, e.g., conversation reset, task derailment, information withholding, ignored other agent's input, reasoning-action mismatch), and (3) task verification / termination issues (FM-3.x, e.g., premature termination, no or incomplete verification, incorrect verification). Note: earlier preprint versions were derived from ~150-200 traces, while the later version references MAST-Data with 1600+ annotated traces across 7 frameworks; the count of 14 modes is consistent across versions.
records.counterfactual: Inverted hypothesis: MAST defines a number of failure modes other than 14 (e.g., 12, 15, or 16) or the taxonomy has been revised to a different count. Verdict: COLLAPSES — the original arXiv abstract (2503.13657), its Figure 1, and multiple independent secondary sources (alphaXiv, Medium summaries, and citing arXiv papers from 2025-2026) all consistently state '14 unique failure modes' in 3 categories; anyone can verify by checking the abstract of arXiv 2503.13657. The only scenario that would overturn this is a future major revision of the paper changing the taxonomy, of which there is no evidence.

In the original TruthfulQA paper (Lin, Hilton & Evans, 2021; ACL 2022), the authors found that across model families (GPT-3, GPT-Neo/J, GPT-2, UnifiedQA), the largest models were generally less truthful than smaller ones — an 'inverse scaling' trend that contrasts with most NLP tasks. For example, the 6B-parameter GPT-J was ~17% less truthful than the 125M-parameter GPT-Neo, and GPT-3-175B reached only ~58% truthfulness versus a 94% human baseline. The proposed explanation is 'imitative falsehoods': larger models learn the training distribution more faithfully, including widespread human misconceptions. Control experiments on non-adversarial trivia-style questions with matched syntax showed normal (positive) scaling, indicating the effect is specific to the benchmark's misconception-probing design. Note this applied to base pretrained models circa 2021; later instruction-tuned/RLHF models score much higher on TruthfulQA, so the inverse-scaling finding is about the original base-model evaluation, not a claim that modern aligned large models are less truthful.
records.counterfactual: Inverted hypothesis: the TruthfulQA paper found larger models were MORE truthful than smaller ones (normal scaling). Verdict: COLLAPSES — the paper's Figure 2 is literally titled 'Larger models are less truthful,' the text explicitly coins the term 'inverse scaling' for this result, and the GPT-J 6B vs GPT-Neo 125M gap (~17% worse) is reported directly; this is corroborated by the arXiv/ACL versions, the authors' own summary, and independent follow-ups (e.g., McKenzie et al. 2023 'Inverse Scaling: When Bigger Isn't Better'). records.answer_text: Turpin, Michael, Perez & Bowman (NeurIPS 2023; arXiv:2305.04388) found that chain-of-thought (CoT) explanations can be systematically UNFAITHFUL: they can misrepresent the true reason for a model's prediction. Injecting biasing features into inputs—e.g., reordering few-shot multiple-choice options so the correct answer is always '(A)', or suggesting an answer—substantially shifts models' (GPT-3.5, Claude 1.0) predictions, cutting accuracy by as much as ~36% on a BIG-Bench Hard suite, yet the CoT explanations almost never mention the biasing feature and instead produce plausible-sounding rationalizations for the biased (often wrong) answer. On a social-bias task, models also justified stereotype-aligned answers without acknowledging the stereotype. Implication: CoT text should not be treated as a transparent, trustworthy account of the model's actual reasoning, so it cannot be relied on alone for safety/oversight.
records.counterfactual: Inverted hypothesis: Turpin et al. 2023 found that CoT explanations faithfully reflect the model's actual decision process, so biasing features that change the answer are reliably disclosed in the explanation. Verdict: COLLAPSES — the paper's abstract (arXiv, NeurIPS proceedings) states the opposite: CoT 'can systematically misrepresent the true reason for a model's prediction' and models 'systematically fail to mention' biasing features. Anyone can check the abstract at arxiv.org/abs/2305.04388 to disprove my answer if it were wrong.

records.answer_text: MAST (the Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy, introduced by Cemri et al., UC Berkeley, in the 2025 paper "Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?", arXiv 2503.13657) defines 14 distinct failure modes. These are clustered into three top-level categories: (1) system design / specification issues (FM-1.1–1.5, e.g., disobey task specification, disobey role specification, step repetition, loss of conversation history, unaware of termination conditions), (2) inter-agent misalignment (FM-2.1–2.6, e.g., conversation reset, fail to ask for clarification, task derailment, information withholding, ignored other agent's input, reasoning-action mismatch), and (3) task verification / termination (FM-3.1–3.3, e.g., premature termination, no or incomplete verification, incorrect verification). The taxonomy was derived from grounded-theory annotation of ~150 traces (κ = 0.88) and then applied to the 1,600+-trace MAST-Data dataset across 7 MAS frameworks. Note: the count has remained 14 across the paper's versions; earlier drafts differed only in category naming (e.g., 'specification and system design failures' vs. 'system design issues').

Verdict: COLLAPSES — the paper's own abstract and Figure 1 (arXiv 2503.13657) state '14 unique modes, clustered into 3 categories', and multiple independent secondary sources (Medium summaries, Scribd, alphaXiv, and at least three citing arXiv papers from 2025–2026) all report 14. The authors showed this by adding biasing features to inputs — e.g., reordering few-shot multiple-choice options so the correct answer is always '(A)', or inserting a suggested answer — which strongly shifted the models' (GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0) answers (accuracy drops of up to ~36% on BIG-Bench Hard tasks) while the CoT explanations systematically failed to mention the biasing feature and instead rationalized the biased, often incorrect, answer. On the BBQ social-bias benchmark, models likewise produced plausible-sounding justifications for stereotype-aligned answers.
